About: Work–Energy Theorem — the Area IS the Energy

Source

Concept
The area under the F–x graph IS the kinetic energy gained — one number, drawn two ways.
Serves
Work as a dot product; the work–energy theorem as an identity; perpendicular forces do no work.
Inquiry
What happens to a moving body's speed if the applied force is exactly perpendicular to its motion?
Misconception
"Any force applied to a moving object changes its speed."

Guided Inquiry

1 · Notice the two panels

On the left, a 2 kg block moves right at 3 m/s on a frictionless surface. A 20 N force pushes it along the motion. On the right you see the F–x graph: force on the vertical, distance on the horizontal.

Press Play. Watch the shaded rectangle under the force line fill in AS the block slides, and the green KE bar grow beside it.

2 · Predict — push perpendicular

Reset and think first. The block is moving right at 3 m/s. Now you push straight up, at 90° to the motion, with a 20 N force through 2 m of travel.

What happens to the block's speed?

3 · Test it

Set the angle to 90° and press Play. The force arrow points straight up; the shaded area under the graph stays at zero; the KE bar does not move; the speed readout holds at 3.000 m/s.

Try any force from 5 N to 40 N at 90°. The area is still zero. Only the component along the displacement does work.

4 · Now tilt it back

Set the angle to 60°, F to 20 N. The shaded area is F cos 60° · d = 20 J — half of what it was at 0°. The KE bar grows to match, tick for tick.

Only cos θ of the force does work. That factor is the whole story of "work is a dot product".

5 · Predict — double the work

At 0° and F = 20 N through 2 m, the block goes from 3 m/s to 7 m/s (KE: 9 J → 49 J, W = 40 J).

If you double the work to 80 J (F = 40 N at 0°), what is the new final speed?

6 · One number, two pictures

The shaded rectangle on the F–x graph and the growth of the green KE bar are literally the same number. That equality is not a coincidence of this setup — it is the work–energy theorem:

Wnet = ΔKE

Explore freely now — change F, θ and m, and check that the two numbers agree every time.

Work–Energy Theorem

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A block slides along a smooth track at 3 m/s while a force pushes it through 2 m. A graph shades the area under the force, and a bar beside it shows the block's kinetic energy.

What you'll learn

  • What the work done by a force means, and how a graph shows it.
  • How to work out the work done by a push at a chosen angle.
  • How to find the block's final speed from the force you apply.
The block moves to the right. The push F makes an angle θ with the direction of motion.

What's on screen

  • F amber arrow: the push. Its length shows the size. A dashed amber line along the track appears once θ is above 0.
  • v blue arrow: the block's speed, with its value beside it.
  • Shaded area on the F–x graph, and, in the bar on the right, the KE₀ starting energy (blue) and the ΔKE growth (green).

03

Work from force and distance

A steady force F that pushes along the motion through a distance x does work W = F x, in joules. On the F–x graph the force is a flat line at height F, so the work is the area of the rectangle under it, from 0 to x.

W = F · x
With F = 20 N, the area reads 20 J per metre of travel

At the opening values, the block moves 2 m under 20 N, so the area ends at 20 × 2 = 40 J. Double the force and the rectangle doubles in height, so the area doubles too.

The graph's vertical axis is labelled F·cos θ. At θ = 0 that is just F.

See itSet F = 30 N with θ = 0° and let the run finish. Watch for: the amber line at 30 N, and the shaded area growing to 60.00 J at 2 m.
04

Force at an angle to the motion

Only the part of F along the motion does work. That part is F cos θ, so the work is a dot product.

W = F⃗ · d⃗ = F d cos θ
The graph plots F cos θ, so its area is this W

At F = 20 N and d = 2 m: θ = 0° gives 40 J, θ = 60° gives 20 × 2 × 0.5 = 20 J, and θ = 90° gives 0 J.

A force at right angles to the motion does no work, however large it is. The speed stays at exactly 3.000 m/s even with F = 40 N. That is why the tension in a string does no work on a stone whirled in a circle, and a magnetic force does none on a moving charge.

A real block pushed upward at 90° with 40 N would leave the ground. The sim holds it on the track, so only the work idea is on show.

See itSet F = 20 N, then θ = 60° and let the run finish. Watch for: the dashed line shorter than the arrow, and the area ending at 20.00 J, half of 40 J.
See itSet F = 40 N and θ = 90°. Watch for: the note "no work", the area staying at 0.00 J, and the speed holding at 3.000 m/s.
05

Work changes the kinetic energy

The weight and the track's push on the block are at right angles to its motion, so they do no work. The net work is the work of F, and it equals the change in kinetic energy.

Wnet = ΔKE = ½mvf² − ½mv₀²
vf = √( v₀² + 2W/m )
The work–energy theorem

At the opening values KE₀ = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J. Adding W = 40 J gives 49 J, so vf = √(2 × 49 / 2) = 7.000 m/s. The shaded area and the green growth of the bar are both 40 J, on the same joule scale.

W does not depend on m, but the speed does. A 4 kg block also gains 40 J and ends at 5.385 m/s. The sim finds v from this theorem, so the two numbers agree by construction.

These numbers follow the sim's sliders.

See itUse the opening values F = 20 N, θ = 0°, m = 2 kg. Watch for: the shaded area and ΔKE both at 40.00 J, and the speed ending at 7.000 m/s.
06

What more work does to the speed

Since KE = ½mv², the speed is not in proportion to the work. At F = 40 N the work doubles to 80 J. The energy goes from 9 J to 89 J, so vf = √89 = 9.43 m/s, not 14 m/s.

Doubling the speed means four times the kinetic energy. From 3 m/s to 6 m/s a 2 kg block needs ΔKE = 36 − 9 = 27 J. Going on from 7 m/s to 14 m/s needs 196 − 49 = 147 J more.

The same rule governs stopping. A steady braking force F over a distance d removes F d = ½mv², so a car at twice the speed needs four times the stopping distance.

See itSet F = 40 N with θ = 0° and m = 2 kg, and let the run finish. Watch for: the area ending at 80.00 J and the speed at 9.434 m/s, well short of 14.
07

Where it matters

  • Circular motion. Tension, and gravity on a satellite in a circular orbit, point at right angles to the motion. They bend the path and never change the speed.
  • Braking. The work of the brakes must equal the kinetic energy, so stopping distance grows as v².
  • Carrying a load. A porter who carries a bag at steady speed along level ground does no work on it, because the lift is at right angles to the motion.
  • Finding speeds. Where the force or the path is awkward, the theorem gives v from the work and the energy alone.
08

Summary

In one line. A block is pushed along a smooth track, and the sim shows a shaded graph area beside the block's kinetic energy.

Key points

  • W = F d cos θ: only the part of F along the motion does work.
  • The shaded area under the F cos θ graph is the work W.
  • Wnet = ΔKE, so vf = √(v₀² + 2W/m).
  • KE goes as v², so doubling the work does not double the speed.

Common mix-ups

  • "Any force on a moving block changes its speed." A force at right angles to the motion does no work and leaves the speed alone.
  • "Double the work gives double the speed." It gives double the energy added, and the speed goes as the square root of the energy.
  • "A heavier block gains less work." The work is the same. The same energy gives a heavier block a smaller speed.

Things to try on your own

  • Set θ = 60° and F = 40 N. Predict the area (40 J) and the speed (7.000 m/s, as in the opening run), then check.
  • With F = 20 N and θ = 0°, change m from 1 to 4 kg. The area stays at 40 J while v falls.
